title: Zedekiah's Request and the Way of Life and Death
summary: With Nebuchadnezzar's army besieging Jerusalem, King Zedekiah sends two officials to ask Jeremiah whether the LORD will work a wonder and drive the Babylonians away. Jeremiah answers that God himself will fight against the city, and that the king and survivors will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar. He sets before the people the way of life and the way of death: stay and die, or surrender and live. The chapter closes with a call to the house of David to do justice every morning.
story: The book now jumps forward. Chapters 11 to 20 mostly reflect the years of Jehoiakim; chapter 21 lands in the final siege, around 588 BC, under the last king of Judah. Everything Jeremiah warned about for decades is happening. This chapter opens a section (21:1 to 23:8) that gathers Jeremiah's words about the kings of David's line, and it is placed first so that the reader sees the end before hearing the reasons: chapter 22 then goes back through the recent kings one by one, and 23:1-8 promises a righteous branch of David to replace them. It is also the first of several scenes in which Zedekiah comes to Jeremiah hoping for a better word (compare 37:3-10, 17; 38:14-28).
historical:
Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC after the surrender and exile of his nephew Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:17). He ruled as a Babylonian vassal but eventually rebelled, and Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem beginning in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4), usually dated to January 588 or 587 BC. The siege lasted about eighteen months, briefly lifted when an Egyptian army approached (37:5-11), and ended with the city's fall in 587 or 586 BC. “Chaldeans” (verse 4) was the common biblical name for the Babylonians, taken from the Chaldean tribes of southern Mesopotamia from which Nebuchadnezzar's father, Nabopolassar, had risen to found the dynasty.

The two messengers are known elsewhere. Pashhur son of Malchijah (a different man from the Pashhur of chapter 20) later demands Jeremiah's death (38:1-4). Zephaniah son of Maaseiah was the second-ranking priest (52:24), sent to Jeremiah again in 37:3. Their hope for “His past wonders” (verse 2) most likely recalls 701 BC, when the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah and withdrew after the angel of the LORD struck his army (2 Kings 19:35-36; Isaiah 37). Zedekiah wanted a repeat.
cultural:
Consulting a prophet before or during a war was standard practice in Israel and throughout the ancient Near East, where kings routinely sought oracles from prophets, priests, and diviners about the outcome of battle (compare 1 Kings 22). Zedekiah's request is conventional; what is shocking is the answer. The phrase “with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm” (verse 5) was the language of the exodus, where God fought against Egypt for Israel (Deuteronomy 4:34; 26:8). Here the phrase is turned around: God fights against his own city.

The king was the chief judge of his people, and hearing cases “every morning” (verse 12) reflects the practice of holding court at the start of the day, often at the city gate or in the palace. Protecting the victim of robbery, the poor, and the powerless was the core duty of every ancient Near Eastern king; law codes and royal inscriptions from Mesopotamia boast of it. Verse 9 uses a soldier's idiom: the one who surrenders will have “his life like a spoil of war”, meaning he will escape with nothing but his life, and that will be his only plunder.
literary: The chapter has a prose narrative frame (verses 1 and 2), Jeremiah's reply to the king (verses 3 to 7), a word to the people (verses 8 to 10), and a poetic oracle to the royal house (verses 11 to 14). The reply to the king reverses every expectation: the weapons of Judah will be turned against itself, God will gather the enemy inside the city, and the holy war traditions of the exodus now point at Jerusalem. The word to the people echoes Deuteronomy 30:15-19, where Moses set before Israel life and death, but where Moses meant obedience to the covenant, Jeremiah now means surrender to Babylon. The final oracle mocks the city's confidence in its high, rocky site with a quotation (“Who can come against us?”) and answers with fire in the forest, perhaps a reference to the royal buildings paneled with cedar (compare 22:6-7, 14).

outline.t: God will fight against the city
The way of life and the way of death
To the house of David: do justice every morning
Against the city that says: who can come against us?

doctrines.note: God is not a national mascot who must defend his city. When his people break covenant, the same arm that rescued them from Egypt can be raised against them. Judgment begins with the household of God.
Nebuchadnezzar's siege is God's work: “I will assemble their forces in the center of this city.” The chapter sees the empire's armies as instruments in God's hand, not as rivals to his power.

The call to the house of David to administer justice every morning shows what God's kingship through David was meant to be: protection of the vulnerable. The failure of the kings to do this is the reason the dynasty falls.

words.note: Pala, to be wonderful or extraordinary; in verse 2 its related form describes God's “past wonders”. The word is used for the great acts of the exodus (Exodus 3:20) and for deeds beyond human power. Zedekiah hoped God's wonders were a resource he could call on. Jeremiah's answer shows that wonders are not a guarantee for a people who will not listen.

Derekh, way, road, or manner of life. “The way of life and the way of death” (verse 8) is the language of choice found throughout the Bible's wisdom literature and in Deuteronomy. The word pictures life as a road with real forks, where direction determines destination. Here the fork is concrete: stay in the city or go out to the besiegers.

Mishpat, justice, judgment, the right ordering of relationships, especially the defense of the weak in court. “Administer justice every morning” (verse 12) makes it the daily work of a king. In Jeremiah, mishpat is what God delights in (9:24) and what the kings of David's line have failed to provide.

christ: The chapter shows a son of David who asked for rescue while refusing to do justice, and it prepares for the promise of 23:5-6, where God will raise a righteous branch for David who will reign wisely and do justice. That king's name, “The LORD Our Righteousness”, is a play on Zedekiah's own name, which means the LORD is my righteousness. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as the son of David who fulfills that promise. The choice between two ways also echoes in Jesus' teaching about the narrow way that leads to life and the broad way that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13-14). And when Jesus foresaw another siege of Jerusalem, he too told his followers to flee rather than trust the city's walls (Luke 21:20-21). These are thematic links, not predictions in this chapter.

hard.q: Wasn't Jeremiah a traitor for telling his own people to surrender to the enemy?
hard.a: His contemporaries thought so. The officials later demanded his death because his words were weakening the soldiers' morale (38:4), and he was arrested on suspicion of deserting to the Babylonians (37:13-14). From a purely political point of view, a public figure urging surrender during a siege is dangerous. Jeremiah's defense is that he was not serving Babylon but speaking what God had said: the city's fall was decided as judgment for its covenant breaking, and those who went out would live. He did not hate his people; the same prophet wept over them (9:1) and chose to stay with the remnant in Judah after the fall rather than accept comfort in Babylon (40:1-6). Readers today may disagree over how far his example applies to any other situation, since his message rested on a direct word from God about a specific judgment. The chapter warns against assuming that loyalty to God and loyalty to one's nation's plans will always coincide.

questions: Zedekiah wanted God to repeat a past miracle without changing anything himself. Where might you be asking God for rescue while holding on to what caused the crisis?
God tells the royal house to do justice “every morning”. What would it look like to make care for the vulnerable a daily habit rather than an occasional project?
Jeremiah's message was unpopular and looked disloyal. How do you tell the difference between faithful dissent and simple contrarianism?
